prompts.q: Name part of marketing's strategic role
prompts.hint: Design, plan, price, promote and distribute... to win what?
prompts.learn: Marketing's strategic role is to maximise sales by developing strategies that design, plan, price, promote and distribute goods and services in an attempt to obtain a competitive advantage.

answers.why: Promotion informs and persuades customers to buy, one of the strategies in marketing's role.
The goal of marketing's strategic role is to maximise sales for the organisation.
Setting the price customers will pay is a core marketing strategy.
Getting goods and services to customers when and where they want them.
Marketing designs goods and services around what customers need and want.
Marketing plans the strategies (the marketing plan) used to reach its objectives.
The whole point: design, plan, price, promote and distribute better than rivals do.

near.msg: Making the product is Operations' role; marketing designs, prices, promotes and distributes it.

prompts.q: Give a way Marketing and Operations depend on each other
prompts.hint: Forecasts one way, specifications the other
prompts.learn: Interdependence is the mutual dependence the key business functions have on one another. Marketing tells operations what customers want and how much will sell; operations sets what can actually be made.

answers.why: Operations relies on marketing's sales forecasts to secure resources and set how much to produce.
Marketing passes market research and design specifications to operations.

answers.a: Ops sets limits on design and specifications
answers.why: Operations may restrict what marketing can promise on design and product specifications.
Marketing, finance and operations work together when designing a new product.
If stock runs out, marketing loses sales, market share and customer satisfaction.
Customising for global markets means different product designs and production, raising costs.
Consistently poor-quality output means complaints and costly warranty claims.

near.msg: Budgets come from Finance, not Operations.

prompts.q: Give a way Marketing and Finance depend on each other
prompts.hint: Money one way, forecasts and sales the other
prompts.learn: Marketing relies on Finance for budgets to fund research and promotion. Finance relies on Marketing for sales and profit forecasts, research for investment decisions and the sales that create cash flow.

answers.why: Marketing relies on finance for budgets to run market research and promotional strategies.

answers.a: Marketing generates sales and cash flow
answers.why: Finance relies on marketing to generate the sales and cash flow that fund the business.
Marketing's sales and profit forecasts feed into finance's key financial statements.
Marketing and finance work together to set prices that sell and still cover costs.
Marketing's market research helps finance make business investment decisions.
Marketing, finance and operations collaborate on new product design.
Implementing the plan needs a financial forecast of costs (research, promotion) and revenue.

near.msg: Recruiting and training marketing staff is the HR link, not Finance.

prompts.q: Give a way Marketing and HR depend on each other
prompts.hint: Source, train, develop, motivate... and who writes the role description?
prompts.learn: Marketing relies on HR to recruit, train, develop and motivate marketing staff. HR relies on Marketing to provide role descriptions and skill requirements so it can source the right people.

answers.why: Marketing relies on HR to source and recruit marketing staff.
HR trains and develops marketing staff, e.g. in product knowledge and customer service.
HR's rewards and policies motivate marketing staff to perform.
HR relies on marketing for role descriptions and requirements so it hires the right skills.

answers.a: Trained staff deliver the People P
answers.why: The People P depends on HR recruiting and training staff who treat customers well.

answers.a: Skilled sales staff for personal selling
answers.why: A sales pitch is only as good as the consultant's skills, which HR recruits and builds.

near.msg: Budgets are the Finance link; HR supplies and develops the people.

prompts.q: Name a feature of the marketing approach (1960s on)
prompts.hint: Stage 1 found out what customers want; stage 2 added CSR, customer orientation and...
prompts.learn: The production (1820s–1920s) and selling (1920s–60s) approaches pushed what the firm could make. The marketing approach finds out what customers want through market research and satisfies it; stage 2 (1980s on) adds CSR, customer orientation and relationship marketing.

answers.why: Stage 1 (1960s–80s) found out what customers want through market research.
Decisions are based on customer wants, aiming to exceed expectations and satisfy customers.
Long-term, cost-effective customer relationships for retention, loyalty and repeat sales.
Stage 2 adds social, environmental and financial outcomes: the triple bottom line.
The idea that the business exists to identify and satisfy customer needs, a focus of stage 1.
In the marketing approach, marketing becomes central to every business function.

near.msg: That's the production approach (1820s–1920s): making goods quickly and cheaply, not asking customers.
That's the selling approach (1920s–60s): advertising and sales reps pushed what the firm could make.

prompts.q: Name a type of market
prompts.hint: CRIMIN
prompts.learn: The six market types are consumer, resource, industrial, intermediate, mass and niche. They differ by who buys and why: final users, producers, resellers, everyone or a narrow group.

answers.why: Individuals buying finished goods for personal use; split into mass, niche and segments.
Mass-produced, mass-distributed and mass-promoted to everyone, e.g. aspirin, petrol, toothpaste.
A small section of the market with a specific need, e.g. gluten-free products.
Businesses buying inputs to make their own products, e.g. Coca-Cola buying cans from Alcoa.
Businesses buying finished goods to resell, e.g. wholesalers, retailers, Woolworths.
Primary producers and extractors: agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining.

near.msg: A segment is a slice of the consumer market, not one of the six market types (CRIMIN).

prompts.q: Name a psychological factor influencing customer choice
prompts.hint: LAMPP (the P in PEGS)
prompts.learn: Psychological factors are influences within an individual that affect buying behaviour: perception, motives, attitudes, personality and learning.

answers.why: How an individual views a business and its product; firms want it seen as quality or innovative.
The reason someone buys, e.g. comfort, safety, taste, fear or cleanliness.
A person's overall feeling about a business or product; a negative one means strategies must change.
Behaviours and traits that shape which brands people buy; products target self-image.
Changes in buying behaviour from information and experience, which can build brand loyalty.

near.msg: That's sociocultural (CRFS): pressure from other people, not from inside the individual.
That's an economic or government factor, not psychological.

prompts.q: Name a sociocultural factor influencing customer choice
prompts.hint: CRFS (the S in PEGS)
prompts.learn: Sociocultural factors are forces exerted by other people and groups that affect an individual's buying behaviour: culture and subculture, reference (peer) groups, family and social class.

answers.why: Society's values, beliefs and traditions shape lifestyle and product choices, e.g. healthy eating.
A person's family role shapes their buying and their say in household purchases.
Peers who influence attitudes, values and beliefs, and therefore purchases.
Education, income and occupation influence the type, quality and quantity of goods bought.
Groups within a culture with their own values; marketing must respect them or risk its image.

near.msg: That's psychological (LAMPP): it comes from inside the individual.

prompts.q: Name an effect of an economic downturn on customer choice
prompts.hint: Think incomes, jobs, and how fussy buyers get about price
prompts.learn: Economic factors are changes in spending and income in the wider economy. In a downturn incomes fall, unemployment rises and buyers become more price-sensitive, so businesses review pricing to hold sales.

answers.why: In a downturn incomes fall, so consumers have less to spend.
Rising unemployment cuts household spending power.
Consumers hold back on purchases when the economy declines.
Customers become more price-conscious and hunt for value.
Confidence and consumption rise in growth and fall in decline.
Firms respond to a downturn by reviewing prices to maintain sales and revenue.

near.msg: That's what happens in economic growth; in a downturn the opposite occurs.
Interest rates are set through monetary policy, the government factor in PEGS.

prompts.q: Name a way government influences customer choice
prompts.hint: FMR (the G in PEGS)
prompts.learn: Government influences buying through fiscal policy (taxes and spending), monetary policy (interest rates) and regulation, e.g. the ACL/CCA enforced by the ACCC.

answers.why: A rise or fall in the cash rate changes how much people borrow and spend.
Changes to personal income tax change disposable income and spending.
Tariffs and excise taxes raise prices and reduce consumption of those goods.
Businesses must comply with the ACL and CCA, enforced by the ACCC.

answers.a: Age restrictions on alcohol and tobacco
answers.why: Laws on who can buy alcohol and tobacco directly limit consumer choice.
Cigarette makers must use plain packaging, limiting how the product can be marketed.

near.msg: That's the economic factor; government acts through fiscal, monetary and regulatory policy.

prompts.q: Give an example of deceptive or misleading advertising
prompts.hint: Before/after, bait and switch, packaging, surveys...
prompts.learn: Under the ACL the dominant message and overall impression of an ad cannot be misleading. Breaches risk ACCC investigation, Federal Court action and fines up to $10 million for businesses and $500,000 for individuals.

answers.why: Distorting the 'before' and enhancing the 'after' to exaggerate results.
Advertising a few cheap items, then steering customers to dearer ones when they run out.
Packaging whose size or shape gives a misleading impression of the contents.
Misrepresenting what a product contains is banned under the CCA/ACL.
Claiming '9 out of 10 people prefer' when no survey was done.
Misrepresenting where a product was made is banned under the CCA/ACL.

near.msg: Puffery is unethical exaggeration, but no reasonable person takes it as fact, so it is usually not illegal.

prompts.q: Name a consumer guarantee or warranty right under the ACL
prompts.hint: Goods: MMF. Services: TFC. Faulty? Three Rs
prompts.learn: Implied conditions are guarantees the ACL builds into every consumer contract, even if never stated. A warranty is a promise to repair, replace or refund faulty products for a reasonable period.

answers.why: A warranty promises to repair, replace or refund faulty products.
Goods and services must do the job they are sold for.
Goods must match their description, sample or demonstration model.
Goods must be safe, durable, free from defects and of acceptable quality.

answers.a: Services done with due care and skill
answers.why: Service providers must do the job competently and carefully.

answers.a: Services done in a reasonable time
answers.why: If no deadline is agreed, a service must be finished in a reasonable time.
No fixed term: based on expected lifespan, price and usage (e.g. phones 2 yrs, cars 5 yrs).

answers.a: Consumer chooses remedy for major failure
answers.why: For a major failure the CONSUMER picks repair, replace or refund.

answers.a: Business chooses remedy for minor failure
answers.why: For a minor failure the BUSINESS picks repair, replace or refund.

near.msg: That's a different consumer law area (WIPD); guarantees cover what the product itself must be.

prompts.q: Name an ethical issue marketers face
prompts.hint: G TAPES
prompts.learn: Ethics are the moral rules governing how businesses operate. The syllabus issues are truth, accuracy and good taste in advertising, products that may damage health, fair competition and sugging; ethical behaviour builds reputation, loyalty and repeat sales.

answers.why: Claims must be true: no concealed facts, puffery or vague statements.
Claims must be precise; ads can be vetted by the ASB and AANA first.
Ads should meet community norms: no over-sexualisation, discrimination or mature content for kids.
Promoting harmful products like junk food to children, cigarettes or alcohol is unethical.
Not using cartels, misuse of market power or exclusive dealing to crush rivals.
Selling Under the Guise of market research, which makes people wary of genuine surveys.

near.msg: That's a consumer LAW (WIPD); ethics covers what's right beyond what's legally required.

prompts.q: Name an unethical marketing practice
prompts.hint: Puffery, vague claims, sex to sell, sugging...
prompts.learn: Truth and accuracy rule out puffery, vague statements and concealed facts; good taste rules out over-sexualised, discriminatory or mature content aimed at children. Wider criticisms include creating needs, stereotyping and invading privacy.

answers.why: Over-sexualised ads breach good taste and community standards.
Junk food ads or mature content aimed at children exploit their naivety and pester power.
Wildly exaggerated claims like 'the best steaks in the world' that no one takes literally.
Ads that perpetuate gender stereotypes or discriminate breach good taste.
Deliberately omitting critical information breaches truth and accuracy.
Unclear, ambiguous claims that can't be pinned down or tested.
E.g. tracking web users' behaviour without their knowledge.
Selling under the guise of market research.
Marketing is criticised for creating wants people didn't have, fuelling materialism.
Embedding brands in shows or films so viewers don't realise they're being advertised to.

prompts.q: Name an anti-competitive practice banned by the CCA
prompts.hint: Cartels, market power, exclusive deals, land...
prompts.learn: Engaging in fair competition means avoiding practices that restrict competition. The ACCC enforces the CCA and lets businesses lodge complaints about rivals' unfair conduct.

answers.why: Competitors agree to act together on price instead of competing.
A dominant firm slashes prices to damage or remove a competitor.
A dominant firm uses its power to damage rivals or block new entrants.
A dominant firm forces suppliers not to sell to its competitors.
Different prices that substantially lessen competition; legal if due to transport costs or local taxes.
Buying up land and retail sites so competitors can't open there.

prompts.q: Give an internal strength or weakness in a SWOT
prompts.hint: Internal = inside the business: people, products, money, equipment
prompts.learn: A SWOT analysis identifies internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. The business then exploits strengths and opportunities and minimises weaknesses and threats.

Strength: products customers already want.

prompts.q: Give an external opportunity or threat in a SWOT

answers.why: Threat: new rivals take sales.

Opportunity: expansion into new markets, including overseas.

prompts.q: Name a stage of the product life cycle
prompts.hint: Intro, growth, maturity... then three post-maturity paths
prompts.learn: The product life cycle is the sequence of stages a product goes through: introduction, growth, maturity, then post-maturity (renewal, steady state or decline). Each stage needs different marketing strategies.

answers.why: Low awareness, slow sales; use intensive promotion and penetration or loss-leader pricing.
Sales rise fast; build brand loyalty and widen promotion and distribution.
Sales plateau in a saturated market; redesign packaging, add features or cut price.
Sales fall; narrow distribution, cut price to clear stock, drop promotion or delete the product.
The stage after maturity, which leads to renewal, steady state or decline.
Post-maturity path where sales are revived, e.g. by modifying the product.
Post-maturity path where sales level off and hold steady.

prompts.q: Name a strategy for a product in the introduction stage
prompts.hint: Awareness, a launch price, and someone else's shops

answers.why: Builds market awareness of a product no one knows yet.

The highest possible launch price targets early adopters and recovers R&D costs.
Selling at or below cost to attract buyers and gain initial share.
Established retailer networks build market share quickly.

prompts.q: Name a common marketing objective

prompts.q: Name a way to implement, monitor or control a marketing plan

answers.why: The pitch adapts to each customer's needs, so a sale is more likely.

Ongoing relationships increase brand loyalty and repeat sales.
Seeing a product work in real life is often more convincing.
One-on-one service can exceed expectations, lifting satisfaction.
A good interaction becomes positive learning (a psychological factor) that drives repeat sales.

near.msg: That's a disadvantage: personal selling is costly, slow and depends on the salesperson's skill.
Reaching a mass audience is advertising's strength; personal selling is one-to-one.

prompts.q: Give an example of a sales promotion
prompts.hint: SPCPR: Start Performing CPR
prompts.learn: Sales promotions are activities or materials used as direct inducements to buy. They encourage trial and create urgency, but add costs and can train buyers to wait for discounts.

answers.why: Discounts on particular items at the time of purchase.
A free item or container of the product to encourage trial.
Special signs, displays and racks installed by the manufacturer in store.
A gift for using the product, e.g. a cookbook with a food product.
Part of the price returned when customers send in proof of purchase.

near.msg: Loyalty programs are relationship marketing, a separate element of the promotion mix.
That's a pricing strategy (the Price P), not a sales promotion.

prompts.q: Give an example of public relations activity
prompts.hint: Press, CSR, charity, sponsorship, issues, crises
prompts.learn: Public relations creates and maintains favourable relationships between a business and the public. Unlike publicity (free news coverage the business can't control), PR is planned by the business, though success isn't guaranteed.

answers.why: Sponsoring a public event links the brand with goodwill.
Donations and charity events build a caring image.
Statements the business sends to the media.
Telling the public about the business's social and environmental work.
Protecting reputation against rumours and adverse publicity before sales suffer.
Early warning of public trends that could hurt sales, so action can be taken in time.

near.msg: That's publicity: free coverage the business doesn't control, whereas PR is planned by the business.

prompts.q: Give an example of an opinion leader
prompts.hint: Influencers, celebrities, business leaders...
prompts.learn: An opinion leader is an individual with influence over a large group of consumers. Endorsements add trust and reach, but they are costly and the brand suffers if the ambassador's reputation is tarnished.

answers.why: Large followings make their referrals powerful.
Celebrity endorsement lends a brand fame and trust.
Sports stars endorsing products to their fans.
Film and TV stars as the face of a brand.
Music stars endorsing products to their fan base.
Respected executives whose views sway consumers.
The ongoing face of a brand; if their reputation is tarnished, so is the brand's.

near.msg: That's word of mouth or a reference group; an opinion leader influences a large group of consumers.

prompts.q: Name a word-of-mouth channel
prompts.hint: Any conversation between consumers, online or off
prompts.learn: Word of mouth is the influence on buying behaviour from conversation. It is trusted and free because it comes from reference groups, but the business can't control it and bad news spreads fast.

answers.why: Consumers trust their reference groups more than advertisers.
Public reviews that influence buying decisions.
Consumers sharing experiences with their followers.
Friends and family talking products over the phone.
Consumers texting each other about products.
Consumers recommending or forwarding by email.
Consumer-written blogs reviewing products.
Online discussion boards where buyers swap experiences.

near.msg: That's paid advertising; word of mouth is consumers talking to each other.

prompts.q: Name a distribution channel
prompts.hint: One direct, three indirect
prompts.learn: Distribution channels are the routes products take from producer to customer: direct, or indirect through retailers, wholesalers and agents. Producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer is the most common for consumer goods.

answers.why: No intermediaries: the producer sends the finished product straight to the consumer.
Often used for bulky or perishable goods like furniture or fruit.
Most common for consumer goods; wholesalers buy in bulk and sell smaller lots to retailers.
Agents earn commission selling to wholesalers; used when a producer has no sales reps.

near.msg: Indirect is a category; name the route: via a retailer, a wholesaler and retailer, or an agent.

prompts.q: Give an advantage of a distribution channel or coverage choice
prompts.hint: Direct, indirect, intensive, selective, exclusive
prompts.learn: Direct channels give control and lower costs; indirect channels tap intermediaries' networks. Channel choice (market coverage) runs from intensive (every outlet) to selective (some) to exclusive (one or a few).

answers.why: Saturating every outlet gives mass coverage and makes buying easy, e.g. milk and lollies.
Cutting out intermediaries can reduce costs.

answers.a: Direct: full control of price and message
answers.why: The business controls price, message and promotional material.
Taps retailers' existing customers and their skilled sales staff.

answers.a: Exclusive: luxury image and higher margins
answers.why: Limited outlets signal status and quality, justifying higher prices and margins.
Dealing directly with customers strengthens relationship marketing and repeat sales.
Specialist distribution businesses can do the job more efficiently.

answers.a: Selective: brand control and wide reach
answers.why: Choosing which retailers stock it widens reach while protecting brand perception.

answers.a: Indirect: foreign subsidiaries for global reach
answers.why: Intermediaries' foreign subsidiaries help a business expand internationally.
Supplying only one or a few outlets cuts transport and logistics costs.

near.msg: Right channel, but name its advantage, e.g. exclusive gives a luxury image.
That's a disadvantage, the flip side of a distribution choice.

prompts.q: Name a physical distribution issue
prompts.hint: WIT
prompts.learn: Physical distribution is all the activities that move products efficiently from producer to customer: warehousing, inventory and transport. Too little stock loses sales; too much raises storage costs.

answers.why: Moving goods by road, rail, sea or air, chosen by product type and service level.
Receiving, storing and dispatching goods from a central organising point.
The stock on hand ready for sale, managed by inventory control systems.
Repeatedly running out loses sales, market share and customer satisfaction.
Carrying too much stock means high storage costs.

near.msg: That's channel choice (market coverage), not physical distribution.

prompts.q: Give an example of physical evidence
prompts.hint: Everything a customer can see, hear, smell or touch around the service
prompts.learn: Physical evidence is the environment in which a service is delivered, plus tangible items like brochures and logos. It should match the positioning, e.g. Apple's premium store locations and design.

answers.why: Design, furnishing, lighting and decoration of the service space.
Staff uniforms signal professionalism and the brand.
Internal and external store signage.
A logo is tangible evidence of a service brand.
Often the first physical evidence a customer sees; it must attract them.
Cleanliness levels shape customer impressions.
Printed material customers can take away.
Where the service is delivered, e.g. Apple's premium store locations.
Business cards and letterheads are tangible service cues.
The sensory atmosphere of the service environment.

near.msg: That's the People P: the quality of staff interaction with customers.
That's Processes: the flow of activities that delivers the service.

prompts.q: Name an e-marketing technology
prompts.hint: Web, pods, texts, blogs, location, social
prompts.learn: E-marketing uses the internet to perform marketing activities. It is cost-effective with global reach and convenience, but criticism is public and visible, so it can be volatile.

answers.why: Popular and effective for younger demographics, but criticism is public.
Customisable and informative, but must be continually updated.
Reaches a large audience fast, but raises privacy concerns.
Online journals that invite feedback and a personal connection, but also negative comments.
Audio or video files distributed to customers over the internet.

prompts.q: Name a global marketing strategy
prompts.hint: GCSCG: Geelong Carlton SCG
prompts.learn: Transnational corporations must adapt their marketing for foreign markets. Global marketing strategies are global branding, customisation, standardisation, competitive positioning and global pricing.

answers.why: One worldwide name, logo or design, giving global recognition.
Very similar strategies in all markets, assuming needs are the same.
Different strategies for each market to meet local needs and wants.
Coordinating prices across countries, shaped by competition, exchange rates, regulation and transport.
Differentiating from rivals through quality products, affordable prices and strong relationships.
Different prices in each country, often to cover export costs like transport and tariffs.
The same price in every market; exchange rate swings can hit profit.
Prices set to suit local demand and competition in each market.

near.msg: Globalisation is the trend; name the strategy a TNC uses (GCSCG).

prompts.q: Give an advantage of standardisation in global marketing
prompts.hint: One product, one message, everywhere
prompts.learn: Standardisation uses very similar strategies in all markets, assuming needs are the same. It is cheaper and easier to manage, but can't meet local needs and is exposed to local competitors; customisation is the reverse.

answers.why: The same promotion and product design can be used everywhere.
A uniform product mix is simpler to run.
Producing one product for all markets cuts unit costs.
One design means less research and development.
Consistency maintains positive perceptions and trust.
Success in one market grows demand elsewhere via reputation and word of mouth.

near.msg: That's an advantage of customisation; standardisation assumes needs are the same everywhere.
